title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
description: Brute force to optimized: a plain array with linear-scan insert/remove versus an array plus hash map using the swap-with-last-element removal trick.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a data structure supporting insert(val) (insert if not present, return whether it was added), remove(val) (remove if present, return whether it was removed), and getRandom() (return a random element from the current elements, each with equal probability), all in average O(1) time.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Uniformly random element in O(1)\"","A plain array is required, since only arrays support O(1) random-index access"],["\"O(1) insert AND remove of arbitrary values, alongside array-based random access\"","Combine an array with a hash map (value to its index), and use the \"swap with the last element\" trick to make removal O(1) too"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

getRandom() needing true O(1) uniform access essentially forces the use of a plain array (since a hash set alone has no notion of "index" to pick randomly from). The challenge is then making remove(val) also O(1), even though removing from the MIDDLE of an array is normally O(n) due to the need to shift subsequent elements.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Numbered Raffle Box With a Seating Chart
blocks.text: Picture a raffle box represented as a numbered list of tickets (for O(1) random draws by ticket number), plus a seating chart telling you exactly which ticket number holds any given name (for O(1) lookup). To remove a ticket without leaving a gap (which would break random draws), you swap it with the LAST ticket in the box before removing the end, keeping the box gapless.

blocks.caption: Removing a middle array element is normally O(n); swapping it with the last element first makes it O(1)

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: insert(1), remove(2), insert(2), getRandom(), remove(1), insert(2), getRandom()

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["insert(1)","true","1 was not present, added"],["remove(2)","false","2 was never present"],["insert(2)","true","2 added, set is now {1,2}"],["getRandom()","1","Some element from {1,2}, chosen uniformly"],["remove(1)","true","1 removed, set is now {2}"],["insert(2)","false","2 already present, not re-added"],["getRandom()","2","Must be 2, the only element left"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before trying to remove elements from an array in place (which normally requires shifting), notice that when the ORDER of elements does not matter (only membership and uniform random access do), a removed element can simply be swapped with the LAST element in the array before popping the array's end, avoiding any shifting entirely.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: getRandom() needing true uniform O(1) access essentially requires a plain array as the underlying storage, since only arrays support direct indexed access.

Observation 2: A hash map from value to its current index in the array gives O(1) lookup, letting insert() check for duplicates and remove() locate a value's position instantly.

Observation 3: Removing an arbitrary array element normally requires shifting everything after it, but since element ORDER within the array does not matter here (only membership and uniform access do), the element to remove can instead be swapped with the array's LAST element, and then the array's last slot can simply be popped off, an O(1) operation.

Observation 4: After this swap, the hash map must be updated too: the value that was moved into the removed element's old slot needs its index entry updated to reflect its new position.

This leads to combining an array (for O(1) getRandom) with a hash map from value to index (for O(1) lookup), and removing an element by swapping it with the array's last element before popping, updating the hash map accordingly.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a plain array. insert() scans to check for duplicates before appending; remove() scans to find the value, then removes it by shifting all subsequent elements left.
Step by step algorithm

items: insert(val): scan the array for val; if not present, append it.
remove(val): scan the array for val; if found, remove it by shifting all later elements one position left.
getRandom(): pick a uniformly random valid index and return that element.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain array directly supports getRandom() in O(1), but insert() and remove() both need a linear scan to check membership, and remove() additionally shifts elements.
This costs O(n) for insert and remove, too slow for up to 2*10^5 calls.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) for insert and remove (scan, plus shifting for remove), O(1) for getRandom.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: adding a hash map for O(1) lookup, and using the swap-with-last-element trick for O(1) removal, brings insert and remove down to O(1) as well.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the hash map matters: a hash map from value to its current array index turns both "does val exist" (for insert) and "where is val" (for remove) into O(1) lookups, instead of O(n) scans.

Why swapping with the last element matters: since the array's element ORDER is irrelevant here (only membership and random access matter), removing an element does not need to preserve position; swapping it with the array's LAST element (moving that last element into the removed slot) and then popping the array's end avoids any shifting entirely.

Keeping the hash map consistent: after the swap, the value that got moved into the removed element's old slot needs its hash map entry updated to point to its NEW index; the removed value's hash map entry is deleted entirely.

The core idea: array plus hash map (value to index), with removal implemented via swap-with-last-element instead of shifting.

Maintain an array and a hash map from value to index. insert() checks the map, appends to the array, and records the new index. remove() looks up the index via the map, swaps that slot with the array's last element (updating the moved element's map entry), pops the array's end, and deletes the removed value's map entry.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for insert(1), insert(2), insert(3), remove(2)

blocks.caption: Array plus hash map; remove swaps the target with the last element, then pops

blocks.text: Why This Works

The hash map gives O(1) existence checks and index lookups, replacing linear scans entirely. Since the array's element order is never semantically meaningful (only membership and uniform random access matter), swapping the element being removed with the array's last element, then popping the array's end, achieves removal without any shifting: the moved element simply needs its hash map entry updated to its new index, and the removed value's entry is deleted. getRandom() remains a simple O(1) random-index array access throughout.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) average for insert, remove, and getRandom.
Space: O(n) for the array and hash map.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) is the canonical example of the "swap with the last element, then pop" trick for achieving O(1) array removal when element order does not matter, combined with a hash map for O(1) lookup.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to update the hash map entry for the element that got moved into the removed slot, leaving a stale index.
Trying to remove by shifting elements (the natural but O(n) approach), missing the swap-with-last trick entirely.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["remove(val) where val is the LAST element in the array","The swap is effectively a no-op (swapping an element with itself), and popping still works correctly."],["insert(val) for a val already present","Returns false, and the array/map remain unchanged."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating "since order doesn't matter, swap-and-pop gives O(1) removal instead of shifting" is the key insight to lead with, since it is the non-obvious trick that makes this problem tractable.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "O(1) random access AND O(1) arbitrary removal", think: array plus hash map (value to index), remove via swap-with-last-element.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support duplicate values (Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed), where multiple indices can map to the same value?
How would you make getRandom() weighted by some property instead of uniform?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "O(1) removal from an unordered collection" problem, solvable via the swap-with-last-element trick.
Randomized data structure design problems generally, often combining an array (for random access) with a hash map (for lookup).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The plain-array approach costs O(n) for insert/remove; the array-plus-hash-map approach with swap-and-pop removal costs O(1) average for all three operations, both using O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: array (for O(1) random access) combined with a hash map (value to index) for O(1) lookup, using swap-with-last-element for O(1) removal.
Core Idea: insert appends and records the index; remove swaps the target with the last array element (updating its map entry) then pops the end.
Time: O(n) for insert/remove in the plain-array approach, O(1) average for all three in the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: since order does not matter, removal can avoid shifting entirely via the swap-with-last-element trick.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, clever combination of a hash map and an array, testing awareness of the swap-and-pop technique.
One line memory trick: array plus index map; remove by swapping with the last element, then popping.
